claim: The top permutation-importance predictors of 2-hour PM peak pedestrian volume at 101 Portland intersections are, in order: Strava walking activity (stv_mi), signalized intersections within 1/8 mi (sig_int_em), distance to CBD, retail floor area within 1/8 mi, zero-car households within 1/2 mi, sidewalk length (intersection buffer and 1/2 mi), fall season, commercial area within 1/4 mi, and unmarked crossings — i.e. POI/retail, signalization, CBD proximity and sidewalk supply are the working pedestrian-exposure proxies.

Built-environment features are computed as multi-scale buffer aggregates around each count point (intersection buffer of 100 ft plus 1/8, 1/4 and 1/2 mile rings) using area- or household-weighted aggregation, and the best model mixes scales (features with _em, _qm, _hm suffixes all enter the top-10).

A tuned histogram gradient boosting model with Poisson loss and L1-Lasso selection of 20 features reduces cross-validated RMSE by 12% (89.8 -> 78.7) and holdout RMSE by 19% (108.0 -> 87.9) relative to the Negative Binomial GLM baseline; the same model on the GLM's 10 hand-picked features already cuts holdout RMSE from 108.0 to 92.7.

Log-transforming the count target should NOT be combined with a Poisson-loss boosting model: it worsened HistGB_Poisson RMSE from 73.7 to 106.8 (and HistGB_Squared 94.4, RF 81.8, ExtraTrees 77.2) because the Poisson log-link already handles the scale.

With 81 training sites and 92 one-hot-encoded GIS features, feature selection is mandatory: using all features makes the GLM overfit (test predictions 254x true volumes), L1 Lasso is the best selector (RMSE 79.8, 26% below baseline before tuning), and the optimal subset size is 20-30 features (Lasso RMSE 84.2/81.9/78.9/81.0/79.8 for 10/15/20/25/30).

At the TAZ level in Beijing (686 TAZs, 10,333 pedestrian crashes in 2015), bus-stop count is the most robustly significant POI predictor of pedestrian crash frequency: coefficient ~0.16-0.18 crashes per additional bus stop, p<0.01 in OLS, SLM, SEM and SDM alike.

Only 6 of 11 POI categories are significant for pedestrian crash counts: bus stops, hospitals, pharmacies, restaurants and office buildings are positive, hotels negative; parking lots, schools, supermarkets, banks and parks are not significant — so generic 'total POI' counts mix informative and uninformative categories.

POI features were encoded as raw counts per zone (not per-km2 density, not log-transformed), fitted with a linear OLS on crash counts; this gives only adjusted R2 = 0.269, i.e. POI counts alone explain a modest share of zone-level pedestrian crash variance.

Spatial autocorrelation of zone-level crash counts is strong (Moran's I of OLS residuals = 0.212, z = 10.0) and a spatial error model gives the best AIC (4639 vs 4705 OLS); i.e. neighbor-zone features or spatial lag terms add information beyond the zone's own POI counts.

POI effects are spatially non-stationary: a GWR model (R2 = 0.369 vs 0.269 for global OLS) shows the per-zone coefficient for bus stops ranging from −0.002 to 0.305 and for pharmacies from −0.070 to 1.368, so global linear coefficients for POI proxies understate heterogeneity across a city.

The paper constructs a composite 'pedestrian exposure intensity' indicator from POI attributes, POI intensity, traffic volume and pedestrian walkability, i.e. it uses POI-based proxies (not observed pedestrian counts) as the exposure term in a pedestrian crash-risk model.

The model (VT-NET, VGG16 CNN + Transformer) produces grid-cell-level spatiotemporal crash-risk predictions and uses exposure intensity alongside weather, socioeconomic and built-environment features, with temporal and non-temporal features trained separately.

Predicted high pedestrian-crash-risk cells concentrate in the city center, persist for several hours, dissipate late night/early morning, and cluster more strongly on weekends in areas coinciding with commercial, public-space, educational and medical POIs — i.e. these POI categories are the ones associated with elevated pedestrian crash risk.

The abstract reports no quantitative effect sizes, feature-importance values, or feature-encoding (density/share/log) recommendations; those would only be available in the paywalled full text (ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403), so the source confirms the proxy design but not its measured effect.

Edge betweenness centrality combined with distance-decay-based node sampling can estimate car AADT per road segment with Pearson r = 0.90 and MAE = 4,100 veh/day against traffic counter data, on a network serving >3 million people (Zurich region, ETH study).

A minimal variant needing only a road-network graph (as available from OSM) and a single distance-decay function reaches 85-90% of the full model's accuracy, i.e. roughly r ~ 0.77-0.81, which makes modified betweenness a viable AADT proxy where no demand model or counts exist.

Plain (unweighted, all-pairs) betweenness is insufficient as a traffic proxy; the paper's contribution is modifying it by sampling origin/destination nodes with a distance-decay kernel (gravity-like trip-length distribution) rather than using the standard all-shortest-paths definition.

Modified-centrality AADT estimation is positioned as a fast, low-data, scalable alternative that trades some accuracy versus full four-step/agent-based demand models; it is appropriate when exposure proxies are needed at scale (e.g. for area-level crash models) rather than when maximum accuracy is required.

The paper estimates AADT for all non-motorway road classes (A, B, C, U) in England and Wales using ~19,000 DfT count points (2016) and 41 predictors (33 numerical, 8 categorical) built in GIS from Ordnance Survey ITN, ONS LSOA socioeconomics, NaPTAN bus/rail stops, VOA land-use records, ports/airports and EV charging points; it does NOT use OpenStreetMap or graph-centrality measures, and number of lanes/speed limits were unavailable.

Area-based exposure proxies (bus stop counts, bus stations, VOA land-use counts, motorway-junction access, charging points) are encoded as raw counts/flags within street-network service areas of six sizes (500, 800, 1000, 1600, 2000, 3200 m), not Euclidean buffers; socioeconomic variables are LSOA means (population density, workplace density, workplace+population density, income, station accessibility share) and sums (population, workplace population, households, registered vehicles). The optimal service area per road class/cluster is selected by lowest MAPE and is mostly small-to-medium (500–1000 m).

Pre-clustering count points with K-prototypes (5 clusters per road class, with min-max normalisation and the AADT target weighted 10 vs predictors 1) followed by per-cluster SVR/RF yields an overall traffic-weighted out-of-sample MAPE of ~14.5% (SVR 14.47%, RF 14.48%, OLS 15.69%); weighted MAPE by road class for SVR is A 14.4%, B 5.7%, C 30.3%, U 27.0%, versus OLS U roads 75.2%. The authors attribute the accuracy gain mainly to clustering plus data transformation rather than to the regression algorithm.

Prediction error is driven by the AADT level of the cluster: low-traffic clusters (rural/minor roads, clusters 4–5) show very high MAPE (up to 276.9% for SVR in C-road cluster 5, 134.6% in U-road cluster 5) despite tiny RMSE (26–68 veh/day), while the highest-traffic cluster has small MAPE but RMSE ~9,000–10,400 veh/day on A roads. Linear regression collapses with small cluster samples (31 points, MAPE 368.7%, RMSE 58,650 on U-road cluster 1).

Administrative road class is an unreliable exposure proxy on its own: the top A-road cluster (96% dual carriageways, 15% ring roads, >10% with motorway access within 800 m) averages ~75,000 veh/day, comparable to motorways (~74,000), and class labels disagree across data sources, so the authors recommend classifying roads by traffic rather than ownership/administrative class.

At ward level in Delhi (289 wards, crashes 2017-19, negative binomial model), wards with higher average betweenness centrality of the OSM street network had fewer crashes, i.e. a negative association between betweenness and crash rate.

Ward-level network structure metrics computed from OpenStreetMap (betweenness centrality, meshedness coefficient, average edge length, node density, average circuity) plus nightlight intensity and population density were used as explanatory variables for a ward-level crash rate negative binomial model.
Nightlight intensity, used as a proxy for ward economic status, was negatively associated with crash rate (poorer wards had higher crash rates).
Wards with higher average circuity (longer network distance relative to straight-line distance) had higher crash rates.
Wards with larger intersection skewness (deviation from 90-degree intersections) and more heterogeneous intersecting road categories had higher crash rates.

At the TAZ level (560 zones, Tehran, 1228 pedestrian crashes 2017-2019), pedestrian exposure was proxied without any pedestrian-volume data using counts/densities of bus stops, schools, pedestrian bridges, intersections, population (total, children, elderly), vehicle and motorcycle ownership, residential/business/recreational land use, road width, lanes, median refuges, sidewalk width, speed, slope and speed cameras; 15 of 25 candidate variables were retained after a first-step screening and pairs with |r|>0.6 were not used together.

In the best-fitting model (GWPR), the proxies with significant positive effects on TAZ pedestrian crash counts were schools (0.104, z=2.88), intersections (0.218, z=6.77), recreational land use (0.201, z=7.72), motorcycles (0.254, z=5.72), vehicles (0.343, z=3.26), road width (0.139, z=4.02), median refuges (0.327, z=7.35) and road slope (0.211, z=7.59); bus stops (-0.355, z=-8.94), total population (-0.312), children (-0.401), residential land use (-0.230), number of lanes (-0.153) and speed cameras (-0.251) were significantly negative.

The sign of several proxy features (bus stops, population density, business land use) flips between model specifications in the same data: bus stops are +0.228 in GWR, -0.084 in GWGR and -0.355 in GWPR; total population is +0.725 in GWR but -0.312 in GWPR; local GWPR coefficients for population range from -2.6 to +5.2 across TAZs, so marginal effects of these exposure proxies are not stable.

A geographically weighted Poisson model on these surrogate exposure features achieves adjusted R-squared of 0.44 (MAD 0.482, RMSE 0.591, Moran's I of residuals 0.031), outperforming GWR (adj. R2 0.41, MAD 0.952) and GWGR (adj. R2 0.32, MAD 0.851), i.e. area-level pedestrian crash counts are only moderately explained by open-data-type proxies without pedestrian volumes.

For the first-step exposure model, keeping all candidate variables in a Tobit (zero-censored) model gave lower error (MAD 22.69, RMSE 37.99) than variable subsets chosen by PCA (Tobit MAD 30.61) or random-forest importance (Tobit MAD 33.76; GLM MAD 31.06), suggesting feature-selection by PCA/RF importance did not improve prediction of pedestrian exposure.

At zonal (macro) level, edge betweenness centrality computed on the road network within each spatial unit is a statistically significant predictor of crash frequency on major roads; all three tested variants (global EBC, local EBC, experiential-hierarchy-based EBC) were significant.

Local edge betweenness centrality (betweenness computed on a spatially restricted sub-network rather than the whole network) shows a stronger association with crash occurrence than global betweenness or hierarchy-weighted betweenness, i.e., restricting the network extent yields a better traffic-share proxy.
Betweenness centrality is used explicitly as a proxy for the share of traffic (exposure) carried by road segments, motivating its use in crash models where direct traffic counts are unavailable.
The study is a zone-level (macroscopic) crash frequency model using 740 Local Self-Governing divisions (Kerala, India) as spatial units, with crash data restricted to major roads.

Network features and demographic characteristics of both the zone itself and its neighboring zones (spatial spillover) are significant predictors of major-road crash frequency, implying neighbor-aggregated features are useful in cell/zone-level models.

In a 500-m grid-cell negative binomial model of pedestrian crashes in Seoul (2015-2017, 2267 cells), the authors use population density and total road length as cell-level proxies for ambient pedestrian population and traffic volume respectively; both are positive and significant (p<0.01) in the all-crash model (Pop_den coef. 0.070 per 1000 people, z=9.73; Road_length coef. 0.061 per 1000 m, z=6.76), and road length stays significant across all severity models including fatal crashes (coef. 0.072, p<0.05).

Proximity to transit is the strongest single predictor in the grid-cell model: the average distance from crash points to the nearest bus stop has the largest z-statistic in the all-crash model (coef. -0.003 per metre, z=-17.07) and is the only transit variable significant for fatal crashes (coef. -0.004, z=-3.86); counts of bus stops (coef. 0.014, z=4.11) and subway stations (coef. 0.110, z=4.60) per cell are also positively associated with total, major- and minor-injury crashes.

Floor area of commercial and office use (per 1000 m2) is positively associated with pedestrian crashes in every severity model (Comm_den coef. 0.006, z=11.00 for all crashes), while single-family housing floor area is negatively associated (coef. -0.002, z=-3.36), i.e. the sign of a 'density' effect depends on land-use type, so building density should be split by use rather than pooled.

Intersection node counts within a 500-m cell are positive predictors of pedestrian crashes: three-way intersections are significant in all four models including fatal crashes (coef. 0.013, z=4.96 for all; 0.028, z=3.28 for death), four-way intersections are significant for all, major and minor injury (coef. 0.029, z=3.61 for all) but not for fatal crashes; a land-use entropy index (LUM, 4 classes) is also strongly positive (coef. 0.511, z=7.15 for all; 0.655 for death).

Pedestrian-attracting POI counts/areas work as activity proxies: number of traditional markets (coef. 0.106, z=6.17), retail store count (coef. 0.016, z=3.08) and hospital floor area (coef. 0.003, z=4.39) are positive and significant for all crashes, while green/open-space area is negative in all models (coef. -0.003, z=-8.32); schools are negative for fatal crashes (coef. -0.125, p<0.05) but positive for minor injuries, which the authors attribute to school-zone speed limits offsetting pedestrian volume.

Several macro-level (zonal) variables — population density, proportions of specific age groups, share of commuters who walk, and share of commuters who bicycle — serve as effective surrogate (proxy) exposure measures for pedestrian and bicycle crashes at intersections, in place of direct pedestrian/bicycle volume counts.

Adding only random effects for the macro-level spatial entity (zone membership) to intersection-level crash models yields a drastic improvement in model fit, and adding zonal covariates improves fit further — i.e., area-level context carries substantial predictive signal beyond site-level variables.

The choice of spatial aggregation unit matters by crash type: ZIP-code tabulation areas (ZCTA) gave the best-performing models for total, severe, and bicycle crashes, while census tracts gave the best pedestrian crash models, among seven geographic units tested.

The study built intersection crash models for four crash types (total, severe, pedestrian, bicycle) using macro-level data from seven different spatial units, coalescing micro-level (intersection) and macro-level (zonal) data in a single modeling framework.

Prior macro-level crash literature consistently finds that demographic and socioeconomic zonal characteristics have substantial effects on traffic safety, but few studies had combined micro-level with macro-level data from existing geographic units before this one.

Among three zonal systems compared for macro-level crash modeling in Florida (census tracts, state-wide traffic analysis zones, and traffic analysis districts), Poisson lognormal models built on traffic analysis districts (TADs) performed best for all three crash categories tested.
Including a spatial autocorrelation term in zone-level Poisson lognormal crash models improves model performance relative to models without spatial effects, regardless of the zonal system used.

Prediction accuracy of zone-level crash models can be compared across different spatial units by re-aggregating predictions onto a common grid, which the authors propose as a grid-based evaluation framework.

The authors recommend using traffic analysis districts (coarser than TAZs) specifically for safety planning, while census tracts remain suited for demographic data and TAZs for transportation forecasting.
As of 2016-2017 there were no established guidelines for choosing the spatial unit (zonal system) for macro-level crash modeling, motivating the comparison.

On real-world road networks (Greater London and five English metropolitan counties, OSM 2019/2021 graphs vs UK AADT counts), plain unweighted betweenness centrality is a weak predictor of AADT; it should not be used as-is as a traffic-exposure proxy.

The best-performing exposure proxy among all tested variants is travel-time-weighted shortest-path betweenness with a 30-minute path cutoff, computed on a primal (intersection-node / road-edge) graph that includes a 30-minute travel-time buffer beyond the study area boundary.

The two modifications that yield the largest gains in correlation with AADT are (a) weighting edges by travel time (i.e., using OSM highway class / speed limits to derive edge costs) instead of topological or pure length, and (b) building the graph with a buffer zone around the area of interest to avoid boundary-effect artefacts in betweenness.

The study is empirical and uses only open data: historical OpenStreetMap road networks (2019 and 2021 snapshots) and the UK DfT public traffic counts (AADT) for 2019 and 2021, evaluating performance by correlation between computed centralities and observed counts.

The thesis is a 2023 Aalto University master's thesis (Mathematics and Operations Research, Complex Systems), i.e., a primary academic source, but not a peer-reviewed journal article; the exact correlation coefficients were not retrievable because the repository host (aaltodoc.aalto.fi) was unreachable during extraction and only abstract text from search snippets was available.

Traffic volume on a road segment can be modeled as a linear combination of two network centrality measures: closeness centrality (proxy for origin-destination trips) and betweenness centrality (proxy for pass-by trips), with road-type-weighted path-distance (PD = Ty*MD) used to compute the centralities.

The centrality-only linear model achieved R2 > 0.92 on validation data in all five cities (Colombo 0.935, Phnom Penh 0.942, Hanoi 0.923, Karachi 0.951, Dar es Salaam 0.959) with median absolute percentage error between 10.5% and 17.3%.
Betweenness centrality alone explains roughly 60% of the variability in segment traffic volume, while closeness centrality alone explains 32-35%; betweenness is the dominant exposure proxy.

Centrality must be computed on a road-type (hierarchy) weighted network: segment cost is path-distance equal to metric length multiplied by a speed factor Ty assigned by road class (expressway/artery/collector/local), rather than pure metric length.

The model coefficients are city-specific and must be recalibrated when transferred to a new area, although the model structure (BC + CC) is retained; the model does not capture seasonal or daily peak variation.

Nighttime light extracted specifically along freeways (SNPP-VIIRS 2015 annual composite, highway-oriented extraction) correlates with provincial freeway traffic flow volume at Pearson r = 0.905 for coaches and r = 0.731 for trucks.

Restricting NTL to the road corridor is substantially more informative about traffic volume than total (area-wide) NTL: the correlation of total nighttime light with freeway traffic flow is only r = 0.593 (coach) and r = 0.516 (truck), versus 0.905 and 0.731 for road-extracted NTL.

The NTL-based Highway Nighttime Traffic Prosperity Index (HNTPI) is strongly collinear with socio-economic variables at the provincial level: Pearson r with GDP per capita 0.772, consumption per capita 0.895, and population 0.968, implying road-corridor NTL largely proxies population/economic activity rather than traffic independently of it.

The NTL-traffic relationship was established using SNPP-VIIRS 2015 annual nighttime light data and validated only at the provincial aggregation level in China (not at segment or grid-cell level), so transfer of the correlation to cell-level crash models is unverified in this source.

Nighttime light along roads is highly spatially heterogeneous and strongest for lower-class national general highways in developed coastal/urban regions (e.g., Shanghai national general highway nighttime prosperity 22.34%), so NTL as an exposure proxy varies in meaning by road class and urbanization.

Using only six Baidu POI count variables (banks, commercial buildings, retail shops, medical services, educational institutions, bus stops counted within a 500 m buffer of each 200 m OSM road segment) as predictors, random forest regression of NKDE vehicle-pedestrian collision density achieved out-of-bag R2 (OOB score) of 0.70-0.84 on arterial, secondary trunk and branch roads in Changning District, Shanghai, but below 0.1 on expressways.

The same POI-only proxies explain vehicle-vehicle crash density well on mid-hierarchy roads (OOB ~0.70 arterial, ~0.80 secondary trunk) but poorly on branch roads (~0.52-0.54) and expressways (<0.1), i.e. POI-based activity proxies substitute for exposure only where trips are local; for long-distance (expressway) traffic they fail.

Adding a single NPP-VIIRS nighttime-light feature (pixel value nearest the segment reference point, ~500 m resolution, nanoWatts/cm2/sr, raw and unstandardized) on top of POI counts raised OOB R2 by +4% to +10% on arterial/secondary roads and +16% on branch roads for vehicle-vehicle crashes (e.g. arterial 0.70 -> 0.77, branch 0.52 -> 0.60), and by 0-6% for vehicle-pedestrian crashes, with NTL showing low collinearity to POI counts (VIF 1.30).

The study's feature encoding was raw counts of POIs within a 500 m buffer around each 200 m road segment plus the nearest NTL pixel value, with no log transform, no density normalization and no standardization, justified by the use of tree-based (random forest) models; collinearity among these counts stayed below VIF 5 (max VIF 4.02 for retail shops).

Normalizing crashes by road length (an exposure proxy available directly from OSM) reverses the apparent ranking of road types: branch roads carry 44.3% of network length and 54.4% of pedestrian collisions (most dangerous per km for pedestrians), while expressways carry 19.6% of length but only 0.7% of vehicle-vehicle crashes.

At the census-block-group level in Lincoln, NE (2,171 motorized-to-non-motorized crashes, 2011–2020), non-motorized exposure ('active miles' from calibrated StreetLight LBS data) correlates more strongly with crash counts (r=0.76) than vehicle miles (r=0.58), poverty rate (r=0.29) or non-white share (r=0.13, p=0.09).

When LBS activity indices are calibrated against intersection counts, land-use/road proxies add little beyond the activity index for pedestrians and vehicles, but matter for bicycles: random-forest feature importance for the StL volume index is 0.660 (pedestrian) and 0.785 (vehicle) vs 0.379 (bicycle), with number of lanes consistently second (0.128 / 0.048 / 0.253) and road network density third for bicycles (0.165).

Raw LBS indices are far weaker proxies for non-motorized than motorized volume: StreetLight vehicle index vs. counts R2≈0.90, pedestrian R2≈0.60, bicycle R2≈0.25; adding EPA-SLD census-block-group covariates (population, occupied housing units, zero-car household share, employment) in linear regression lifts adj-R2 to 0.91 / 0.78 / 0.37 for vehicle / pedestrian / bicycle.

In a spatial-lag model of area-level non-motorized crash rate (crashes / (active miles × vehicle miles), 187 CBGs, pseudo-R2=0.23), multimodal network density (facility miles per sq mi) is the strongest positive predictor (effect size +112% per SD, p=0.00), while employment entropy (-89%, p=0.00), employment density (-76%, p=0.00), weighted intersection density (-59%, p=0.06) and walkability index (-68%, p=0.07) are negatively associated; one-car household share and low-wage worker share are positive (~+79%, p=0.01).

The sign and significance of area-level land-use/density features depend on which exposure normalization is used (crashes/(active×vehicle miles), crashes/(active/vehicle ratio), crashes/active miles): e.g. three-leg multimodal intersection density is positive and significant under ratio (effect +57%, p=0.00) and active-miles (+17%, p=0.005) rates, while auto-removed intersection density is negative under multiplicative (p=0.06) and active-miles (p=0.029) rates; the report also warns that aggregating segment volumes to block groups inflates area volume when only a few segments carry traffic, and recommends effect sizes standardized per 1 SD because raw density variables were rescaled by 10,000.

Using population (or population density) as a surrogate for pedestrian exposure in zonal pedestrian-crash models yields biased coefficient estimates: effects of several risk factors differed substantially between population-based and activity-based exposure models in 209 Hong Kong neighborhoods.

Among four pedestrian exposure measures (population, walking trips, walking time, walking distance), the model using number of walking trips had the best goodness-of-fit in a Bayesian spatially varying coefficients model of pedestrian-motor vehicle crash counts.

After controlling for vehicle volume and pedestrian activity, road density, intersection density, bus stop density, and number of parking lots are positively associated with zonal pedestrian-motor vehicle crash frequency, while share of motorways and median monthly income are negatively associated.

Spatial heterogeneity in covariate effects (spatially varying coefficients) is non-negligible when modeling crashes over contiguous zones; heterogeneity arises from spatially correlated effects, not only unstructured variability.
Pedestrian exposure at zone level can be derived from crowdsourced travel-diary data by extracting pedestrian trajectories and aggregating them to neighborhoods (209 units in Hong Kong).

In a crash-level injury-severity model for Changsha (2017–2019), SHAP on a CatBoost model ranked distance to nearest metro station first, road network density (per 1 km grid) third, POI mix (Shannon index within 1,000 m) fourth and distance to nearest bus stop fifth among all predictors, and 5D built-environment variables accounted for roughly 75% of total SHAP value.

Built-environment (5D) features alone are weak predictors of injury severity given a crash: CatBoost with 5D-only features reached ROC-AUC 0.774, versus 0.924 with crash-context (non-5D) features and 0.941 with both combined.

The exposure/accessibility proxies were encoded as: road network density = total road length divided by grid area on a 1 km × 1 km grid (resolution chosen to match the 1 km population raster); POI mix = Shannon diversity index of POI categories in a 1,000 m buffer; destination accessibility = raw counts of schools, hospitals, malls, tourist attractions within 1,000 m; transit access = continuous distance in km to nearest metro station and bus stop.

Effect directions: injury risk increases nonlinearly with distance from the nearest metro station, while higher POI functional mix and higher road network density are associated with lower injury risk (SHAP shifts from positive to negative).

CatBoost with native categorical handling outperformed XGBoost and Random Forest (both with SMOTE) on the same feature set: ROC-AUC 0.941 vs 0.929 vs 0.926; residual spatial autocorrelation was weak (Moran's I = 0.074, p < 0.001).

Measurement error in traffic volume (the most common exposure predictor in safety performance functions) attenuates the estimated effect of that predictor toward zero and inflates overdispersion — i.e. a noisy AADT proxy will yield a biased-low exposure coefficient and more apparent unexplained variance.

A negative binomial SPF that explicitly models measurement error in traffic volume (MENB, using a measurement-error model built from traffic-flow time-series data) outperforms the standard negative binomial SPF in Monte Carlo simulation when measurement errors are large.

When traffic volume is measured with error, the conventional NB SPF systematically underestimates predicted accident counts for high-volume, long road segments and overestimates them for low-volume, short segments — the bias is not uniform but depends on exposure magnitude.
The method was estimated with full Bayes MCMC and applied to two empirical datasets of 131 and 130 road segments in British Columbia, Canada (segment-level, not area/cell-level).

In a 250x250m grid model of Barcelona accidents, exposure/activity proxies (traffic variation and mobile-phone footfall) were the strongest SHAP drivers, ahead of infrastructure features (traffic lights/signs), POI density and road-type index.

Road class and speed limit were encoded per cell as length-weighted indices (road type × length, speed limit × length in each cell) rather than raw counts, and intersections as a composite of count plus mean distance to the 3 nearest intersections.
The standard deviation of hourly traffic within a cell was used as a proxy for peak/variable traffic exposure and emerged as the top feature.
A Regression Kriging model with a Random Forest regressor on 250x250m cells achieved R2 = 0.71 for accident prediction.

The feature set combined open data (OSM building footprints and road intersections, municipal accident and signaling data) with premium data (TomTom traffic, POI by trade division, Vodafone footfall, working population), so the strongest exposure proxies here were NOT derived from open data alone.

In a leave-one-out ablation on OSM-derived road graphs (DE, MA, MD, NV), removing graph-structural features (node in/out-degree and betweenness centrality) lowers accident-classification AUROC by about 6.9% on average, a larger drop than removing weather (2.3%) or measured AADT traffic volume (1.2%); e.g. NV falls from 91.62 to 82.56 AUROC and MD from 87.51 to 79.77 without structural features.

OSM road category (24 binary tags: oneway, motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary, residential, living street, link roads, unclassified, etc.) plus road length is the second most important feature group: dropping 'road information' cuts AUROC from 87.61 to 82.99 (DE), 87.51 to 80.63 (MD) and 91.62 to 84.24 (NV), while dropping official AADT changes AUROC by at most ~1.3 points.

Official AADT is available for only ~1.3-3.1% of OSM road segments in the states where it exists at all (DE 3.14%, MA 1.34%, MD 1.76%, NV 1.38%; none for IA, IL, MN, MT), which is why the authors treat volume as an auxiliary transfer-learning target rather than a primary input; using AADT prediction as an auxiliary task gives a relative gain of 1.1% AUROC and 7.9% MAE over single-task learning.

Recommended encodings in the benchmark: node in-degree and out-degree as one-hot vectors (dimension = graph max degree, ~6-8), betweenness centrality as a real-valued fraction of shortest paths, road length in meters as a raw real value, road category as a 24-dim multi-hot vector, and AADT as a yearly real-valued average vehicle count; no log transform or density normalisation is applied.

A plain MLP on the same node features (degrees, betweenness, weather) without graph message passing achieves only 56-77 AUROC per state, whereas GraphSAGE over the OSM graph reaches 82-92 AUROC (average ~87%), with positive rates of only 0.05-0.23% of edges per month; Node2Vec/DeepWalk embeddings alone already lift MLP to ~70-92 AUROC, showing neighbourhood/structural context is the dominant signal.

A quantile regression forest trained on ~99k road segments with empirical AADT from 46 countries, using only open/global predictors (road class, population density at several scales, GDP/HDI, travel-time-weighted betweenness centrality), reaches pseudo-R2 ≈ 0.74 on a 20% hold-out set, i.e. open-data proxies explain roughly three quarters of the variance in log-AADT on extra-urban roads.

Road type (highway/primary/secondary) is by far the strongest single predictor of traffic volume, with GDP per capita, large-radius betweenness centrality (eBetw240) and population within a 2 km circle around the segment the next most important variables.

Betweenness centrality of the road graph, weighted by travel time and computed at two cutoff scales (60 and 240 minutes), is a useful exposure proxy because it separates short-distance and long-distance through-trips on a segment.

AADT should be modelled on a natural-log scale because the empirical distribution is strongly right-skewed; population-type predictors are built as multi-scale aggregates (local 2 km radius vs. larger neighbourhoods) rather than a single density value.

Empirical traffic counts cover only ~3% of the extra-urban road network even in a 46-country compilation, which is why model-based AADT proxies are needed; the resulting global dataset exists for 1975, 1990, 2000 and 2015 but historical layers are less reliable.

Across contiguous US counties, OSM road length is almost always lower than Census TIGER road length: the completeness ratio R_t = L_OSM / L_TIGER is below 1 in nearly all counties, with only seven counties exceeding 1 — so OSM-derived road-density / network features systematically undercount roads relative to the official baseline.

OSM road data completeness and positional accuracy are significantly better in metropolitan counties than in nonmetropolitan and rural counties (ANOVA on mean R_t: F = 74.28, p < 0.05), implying OSM-based exposure proxies carry an urban/rural bias that confounds comparisons between dense and sparse zones.

OSM road-data quality is spatially clustered rather than randomly distributed across counties (global Moran's I = 0.558, p < 0.001), with low-low clusters concentrated in the western US — so OSM measurement error in area-level models is spatially autocorrelated and can be absorbed into regional/spatial effects.

Positional accuracy of OSM roads was measured as the share of OSM road length falling within 1–5 m buffers of TIGER roads (individual-buffer ratio R_i and dissolved-buffer ratio R_d), and metro/nonmetro/rural differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) at every buffer distance — relevant when snapping crashes or POIs to OSM segments or computing cell-level road length.

The authors state that inconsistent OSM road completeness can materially change the output of downstream applications that take the road network as input, which is a caveat for using OSM graph metrics (centrality, density) as exposure proxies in crash models.

At the TAZ (traffic analysis zone) level, a spatially-weighted XGBoost (Geo-XGBoost) that encodes geographic proximity of neighboring zones outperforms non-spatial tree ensembles (Random Forest, GradientBoostingRegressor, LightGBM, XGBoost) for crash-count prediction, with RMSE reduced by 1.17%-23.14%, MAE by 0.42%-24.74%, and R2 improved by 2.42%-45.03%.

Zone-level road network pattern features (grid-like suburban layouts and high-accessibility road networks) are among the strongest correlates of crash risk, i.e. network-structure/accessibility proxies carry real predictive signal in area-level crash models.

The model combines static road-network-pattern features with dynamic traffic-flow (exposure) features at the TAZ level and uses interpretable ML (post-hoc explanation) to recover feature-crash relationships, rather than relying only on network structure.

Area-level crash models that assume spatial homogeneity and uniform neighbor influence underperform; explicitly modeling nonlinear spatial dependence and local variation (spatial weighting of neighbors) is needed when using zonal network/exposure proxies.

A trivial baseline using only the OSM road class (highway tag), 'class_only', is the best or near-best uncalibrated predictor of car counts in several cities: Spearman rho = 0.779 (Oxford), 0.673 (Melbourne), 0.706 (Toronto), 0.593 (Leeds), 0.544 (Zurich), beating OD-based centrality/assignment tools (cityseer, AequilibraE) in Oxford and Melbourne.
For heavy-vehicle flows, the OSM road-class-only baseline wins in every case with heavy counts (Leeds rho 0.571, Melbourne 0.574, Oxford 0.619, Toronto 0.68), ahead of betweenness/OD-based tools.

For pedestrian flows, a simple OSM POI 'attractor_density' baseline (rho 0.589 Oxford, 0.622 Melbourne, 0.548 Toronto) massively outperforms network-centrality / OD-flow tools, which score near zero or negative for walking (cityseer -0.009 Oxford, 0.02 Toronto; AequilibraE -0.062 Oxford, -0.142 Toronto).

For cycling, distance to city centre ('centre_distance') is the best single open covariate in Oxford (rho 0.658), Toronto (0.559), Zurich (0.278) and Leuven (0.259), beating OD-based centrality in each; cycling is predicted worse than car overall (max rho 0.66 vs 0.78).

Where OD-based centrality/assignment (AequilibraE user-equilibrium, cityseer) beats class-only for cars (Leeds rho 0.639, Toronto 0.744, Zurich 0.717), it does so only in rank order: its log-scale R2 is strongly negative (-2.1 to -7.8), so raw centrality/assigned flows are useful as rank proxies for exposure but need calibration (e.g., log transform plus regression) before being used as magnitudes; the benchmark itself scores on Spearman rho and log R2.

On a three-year Hillsborough County (Florida) urban network dataset, a micro-level Bayesian spatial joint model (zonal crashes = sum of expected crashes of road entities in the zone) achieved better overall fit and predictive performance than a macro-level Bayesian CAR zonal model.
Macro-level (zonal) crash models are justified mainly by lower data requirements and suitability for long-term transportation planning, not by superior predictive accuracy.

The paper proposes and empirically evaluates two alternative formulations of zonal crash frequency: aggregating crash statistics to a spatial scale and relating them to macroscopic factors (macro), versus summing expected crashes of all road entities inside the zone (micro).
An integrated hot-zone screening approach that combines separate macro-level and micro-level screening results was proposed to exploit the merits of both levels.

In a random-parameter negative binomial crash-frequency model for Greater Melbourne, zone-level built-environment proxies — employment density, road density, highway (major road) density, job-housing balance, land-use mixture, and bus route density — are statistically significant predictors of crash counts, i.e. density- and share-type encodings of OSM-derivable features carry signal for area-level crash models.

Segmenting the study area into traffic-density-based zones (TDZs) rather than administrative/planning zones yields a better-fitting crash frequency model (improved goodness-of-fit), suggesting that the choice of spatial unit for aggregation materially affects area-level crash modelling.

Dynamic traffic-flow exposure variables derived from the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (shockwave velocity and congestion index) have heterogeneous (random-parameter) effects on crash frequency across zones, so a single fixed coefficient for congestion/flow exposure is inadequate.

The association between zone-level covariates and crash frequency was estimated with a random parameter negative binomial regression, the standard count model family for macro-level crash prediction with overdispersion.
